title: Cervical intra-extradural meningioma with en-plaque, dumbbell-shaped, and an unusual calcified pattern in a young patient
case_prompt: A 22-year-old woman presented with a several-week history of progressive weakness and numbness in both lower limbs. On examination, she had diminished pain and temperature sensation below the T1 dermatome, loss of vibration and proprioception in all extremities, motor strength of 2/5 in the lower extremities, mild weakness of right finger flexion, global hyperreflexia, bilateral ankle clonus, and positive Babinski signs. Cervical MRI showed a lesion extending from C5 to C8 that was hypointense relative to the spinal cord on T1-weighted images and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images. After gadolinium administration, the mass enhanced homogeneously and comprised two portions: an infiltrative intradural component with ill-defined borders and an extradural component. On coronal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images, the lesion formed a dumbbell-shaped expansion through the left C6–C7 and C7–T1 neural foramina. A CT scan of the cervical spine demonstrated macroscopic calcification within the lesion.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Metastasis was considered due to the extradural location but was unlikely given a negative work-up — “In spite of a negative metastatic work-up, physicians should always raise concerns about a cancerous potential when confronting an extradural lesion regardless of age.”  
2. Ependymoma was considered because of the intradural extension suggesting an intramedullary origin but was excluded as ependymomas are strictly intramedullary and rarely calcify — “Spinal ependymomas arise from ependymal cells lining the central canal; therefore, they are strictly intramedullary in location...calcification is uncommon in this entity.”  
3. Glioblastoma multiforme was considered due to the heterogeneous appearance and prognostic implications but was excluded because calcified spinal glioblastomas are extremely rare — “calcified spinal glioblastoma multiforme is extremely rare.”  
4. Nerve sheath tumor (schwannoma/neurofibroma) was considered for the dumbbell shape and enhancement pattern but was excluded since calcified schwannomas/neurofibromas are rare and they seldom involve both intra- and extradural compartments — “The heterogeneous enhanced dumbbell-shaped expansion on the T1W with contrast has posed the likelihood of a nerve sheath tumor...calcified schwannomas/neurofibromas are rare, additionally it is very uncommon for these lesions to have two separated portions in and outside of the dura.”  
5. Meningioma was considered because calcification and homogeneous enhancement on imaging are characteristic of psammomatous meningiomas — “CT scan has a higher sensitivity in detecting psammomatous calcifications; hence, it will provide additional hints for the diagnosis in patients with a hazardous tumor appearance like in our case.”
